paragraphs.title: A Plea to Remember and See the Destruction

easy.explanation: He asks why God has cast His people off forever.
easy.q: What feeling does the psalmist express at the beginning?
Whom does the psalmist ask God to remember?

easy.explanation: The passage names Mount Zion as the place where God dwelt.
easy.q: Which place is mentioned as the place where God dwelt?

medium.explanation: He asks God to come and see what the enemy has done in the sanctuary.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask God to lift up His feet?

medium.explanation: The image describes God’s people as sheep belonging to His pasture.
medium.q: What does “the sheep of thy pasture” refer to in this passage?

answers: As roaring and setting up their ensigns
medium.explanation: The enemies roar in the congregations and set up their signs.
medium.q: How are the enemies described in verse 4?

answers: The psalmist asks God to remember His people and see their condition
The psalmist asks God to forget the sanctuary
The psalmist describes a celebration after victory
challenge.explanation: The plea asks God to notice Israel, Zion, and the devastation caused by the enemy.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the plea to remember and the description of destruction?

answers: The crisis concerns both God’s people and His holy place
The crisis concerns only the enemies
The psalmist is speaking only about nature
challenge.explanation: The passage joins the suffering of the people with the destruction of the place where God dwelt.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from mentioning the congregation, the inheritance, and Mount Zion together?

answers: God’s former redemption contrasts with the present desolation
The sea contrasts with the desert only
challenge.explanation: God had purchased and redeemed His people, but they now face abandonment and ruin.
challenge.q: What major contrast appears in this section?

paragraphs.title: The Destruction of the Temple and Sacred Places

easy.explanation: The enemy is compared to someone lifting axes against thick trees.
easy.q: What kind of worker is used as an image for the enemy?

easy.explanation: The enemy breaks down the carved work with axes and hammers.
easy.q: What does the enemy do to the carved work?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary.”
easy.q: What does the enemy cast into the sanctuary?

medium.explanation: The woodcutting image portrays forceful destruction.
medium.q: What does the description of axes and thick trees emphasize?

answers: They destroy violently and without restraint
They are trying to repair the sanctuary
medium.explanation: The tools show deliberate and violent destruction.
medium.q: What do the axes and hammers reveal about the enemy’s actions?

answers: The sanctuary is defiled and sacred places are burned
medium.explanation: The enemy burns the sanctuary and casts down the dwelling place of God’s name.
medium.q: What is the result of the actions described in these verses?

answers: It presents the ruin as forceful and systematic
It shows that the enemy protects the holy place
It describes the beauty of the sanctuary
challenge.explanation: Repeated blows with axes suggest determined and extensive destruction.
challenge.q: Why does the woodcutter image strengthen the sense of destruction?

answers: Both express an attack on the places of worship
challenge.explanation: The enemy seeks to destroy the visible places associated with God’s worship.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between burning the sanctuary and destroying the synagogues of God?

answers: They intended to wipe out the people and their worship completely
They wanted to join God’s worship
They wanted to preserve the sanctuary
challenge.explanation: Their purpose was comprehensive destruction rather than limited damage.
challenge.q: What does the statement that the enemies wanted to destroy them together suggest?

paragraphs.title: The Absence of Signs and the Cry for Action

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “We see not our signs.”
easy.q: What does Israel no longer see?

easy.explanation: The passage says there is no more any prophet to tell them how long.
easy.q: Who is no longer present to tell them how long the suffering will last?

easy.explanation: He asks why God withdraws His hand, although God works salvation.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do?

answers: The enemy continues to reproach and the suffering continues
medium.explanation: The absence of signs and prophets leaves the people wondering when the suffering will end.
medium.q: Why is the question “How long?” asked?

medium.explanation: The enemy is insulting and dishonoring God’s name.
medium.q: What does “reproach” mean in this context?

answers: God’s hand seems inactive, although He is King and works salvation
medium.explanation: The psalmist knows God’s saving power but asks why it is not being shown now.

answers: Uncertainty about when the suffering will end
challenge.explanation: Without a prophet, no one tells them how long their distress will continue.
challenge.q: What does the absence of prophets contribute to the people’s feelings?

answers: It emphasizes the contrast between His known power and His present silence
It cancels the request for help
challenge.explanation: The title recalls God’s past authority and salvation while questioning His current lack of visible action.
challenge.q: Why is God called “my King of old” in the middle of this complaint?

answers: The continuing insult makes God’s intervention urgent
The insult causes the psalmist to praise the enemy
challenge.explanation: The enemy’s ongoing blasphemy intensifies the plea for God to act.
challenge.q: How are the enemy’s reproach and the request for action connected?

paragraphs.title: God’s Power over the Sea and Creation

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength.”
easy.q: What did God divide by His strength?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions the heads of the dragons and Leviathan.
easy.q: Which creatures are mentioned in this description of God’s power?

easy.explanation: The psalm says God prepared the light and the sun.

answers: The sea, rivers, day, night, earth, and seasons
medium.explanation: The verses describe God’s authority over waters, time, land, and seasons.
medium.q: What does the description of God’s rule over creation include?

answers: They are signs of the enemies
medium.explanation: The phrase describes rivers with great strength or volume.
medium.q: What does “mighty rivers” communicate about the rivers?

answers: They all display God’s authority over creation
They all describe the enemy’s tools
They all concern the absence of prophets
medium.explanation: The passage moves from the sea and waters to time, earth, and seasons.

answers: God rules over both time and space
God rules only over the Temple
The psalmist is speaking only about the enemy
challenge.explanation: Day and night represent time, while the earth’s borders represent space.
challenge.q: What is suggested by mentioning the day and night alongside the borders of the earth?

answers: The psalmist presents a broad range of God’s authority
The psalmist changes to an unrelated subject
The psalmist describes only one disaster
challenge.explanation: The description expands from particular natural forces to the order of the whole world.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the movement from the sea to the seasons?

answers: It reminds the psalmist that God has power to act in the present crisis
It proves that God has no power
It removes the reality of the destruction
challenge.explanation: God’s power over creation implies that He is able to deliver His people now.
challenge.q: Why can recalling God’s power in creation strengthen the plea for action?

paragraphs.title: The Covenant and the Protection of the Poor

answers: The enemy’s reproach and the covenant
easy.explanation: He asks God to remember the enemy’s reproach and to have respect unto the covenant.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to remember?

easy.explanation: He asks God not to forget the congregation of His poor.
easy.q: Whom does the psalmist ask God not to forget?

answers: That they not return ashamed and may praise God’s name
easy.explanation: He asks that the oppressed not return ashamed and that the poor and needy praise God’s name.
easy.q: What does the psalmist desire for the poor and needy?

medium.explanation: The turtledove is a picture of the people whom God is asked to protect.
medium.q: What does “thy turtledove” represent in the passage?

answers: It recalls the binding relationship between God and His people
It cancels the relationship with the people
medium.explanation: The covenant provides a basis for asking God to remember and defend His people.
medium.q: Why does mentioning the covenant strengthen the request for protection?

answers: Deliverance would allow the poor to praise God instead of returning ashamed
Praise prevents them from asking for help
medium.explanation: The psalmist seeks rescue so the poor and needy can praise God’s name.
medium.q: How are protection and praise connected in these verses?

challenge.explanation: The turtledove represents the endangered community placed under God’s care.
challenge.q: What role does the turtledove play in the passage?

answers: Both are presented as matters requiring God’s remembrance and protection
The profaning of God’s name is presented as desirable
challenge.explanation: The psalm connects the enemy’s blasphemy with the suffering of God’s people.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the profaning of God’s name and the people’s suffering?

answers: The crisis is measured partly by the condition of the vulnerable
The poor are not part of God’s people
The psalmist asks God to protect only the enemy
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes God’s concern for those most exposed to suffering.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the special concern for the poor and oppressed?

paragraphs.title: A Final Appeal for God to Defend His Cause

answers: Arise and plead His own cause
easy.explanation: He says, “Arise, O God, plead thine own cause.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do?

answers: The reproach of the foolish man
easy.explanation: He asks God to remember how the foolish man reproaches Him daily.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to remember?

answers: The tumult of those who rise against God
easy.explanation: The verse says that the tumult of God’s enemies increases continually.
easy.q: What continually increases according to the final verse?

answers: Defend God’s honor and answer His reproachers
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks God to act on behalf of His name, sanctuary, and people.
medium.q: What does “plead thine own cause” mean in this context?

answers: The enemies reproach and blaspheme Him
medium.explanation: The enemies’ insults and increasing tumult call for God’s response.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask God to plead His own cause?

answers: It repeats the call for God to intervene after destruction and reproach
It changes to a subject about commerce
It removes the Temple from the poem
medium.explanation: The ending gathers the psalm’s plea for God to act against the enemies.
medium.q: How does the conclusion relate to the main theme of the psalm?

answers: The psalmist makes the plea more urgent: God must not only remember but intervene
The psalmist gives up hope of deliverance
The psalmist asks God to honor the enemy
challenge.explanation: The final appeal turns remembrance into a direct call for action.
challenge.q: What is the significance of moving from asking God to remember to asking Him to arise and act?

answers: The attack on the people and sanctuary is also an attack on God’s honor
The destruction is only a private event
challenge.explanation: The psalm presents the suffering of God’s people and sanctuary as a matter involving God Himself.
challenge.q: What does “thine own cause” suggest about the nature of the destruction?

answers: It emphasizes that the enemies’ threat and noise continue without stopping
It indicates that the enemy has disappeared
It describes the coming of winter
challenge.explanation: The phrase leaves the reader with a strong sense of ongoing and escalating opposition.
challenge.q: How does “increaseth continually” affect the ending?
